body.en: Unit 3 treats trigonometric functions as circular functions defined for all real numbers — not just angles in triangles. The emphasis is on periodicity, transformations, inverses, and polar coordinates.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Radian Measure, Unit Circle & Core Trig Values

body.en: Understand radian definitions of angle measure, determine terminal coordinates on the unit circle, and evaluate exact trigonometric values.

Arc length: \[ s = r\theta \quad (\theta \text{ in radians}). \quad 360^\circ = 2\pi\text{ rad}, \quad 1\text{ rad} = \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}. \]

On the unit circle (\(r = 1\)): \( (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \) represents the terminal point on the circle. Period of \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) is \(2\pi\); period of \(\tan\) is \(\pi\).

Find the exact value of \(\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\).

The angle \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) lies in Quadrant II with a reference angle of \(\pi - \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

In Quadrant II, sine is positive and cosine is negative: \[ \sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}, \quad \cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. \]

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

What is the exact value of \(\tan\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\)?

solution.en:
The angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) lies in Quadrant III with reference angle \(\frac{4\pi}{3} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

In Quadrant III, both sine and cosine are negative, making tangent positive: \[ \tan\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = +\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \mathbf{\sqrt{3}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Sinusoidal Modeling, Amplitude, Period & Phase Shift

body.en: Model periodic phenomena using transformed sinusoidal functions and apply restricted domains of inverse trigonometric functions.

\[ y=A\sin(B(x-h))+k \quad \text{or} \quad y=A\cos(B(x-h))+k. \]
ParameterEffectFormula
\(|A|\)AmplitudeHalf vertical distance: \(\frac{\max-\min}{2}\)
\(B\)Angular frequencyPeriod \(=\frac{2\pi}{|B|}\implies B=\frac{2\pi}{\text{Period}}\)
\(h\)Horizontal (phase) shiftShift right by \(h\)
\(k\)Vertical shift (midline)Midline \(y=k=\frac{\max+\min}{2}\)

\[ \sin^{-1}x:\text{ domain }[-1,1],\text{ range }\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]. \]\[ \cos^{-1}x:\text{ domain }[-1,1],\text{ range }[0,\pi]. \]\[ \tan^{-1}x:\text{ domain }(-\infty,\infty),\text{ range }\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right). \]

These restricted ranges are necessary so that the inverse relations satisfy the definition of a single-valued function.

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Trigonometric & Polar Functions

body.en:
• Radian Mode on Calculator: All AP Precalculus exam questions assume radians unless an explicit degree symbol (°) is provided. Keep your calculator set to Radian mode.
  • Factoring Out Frequency: In \(y = \cos(2x - \pi)\), the phase shift is NOT \(\pi\); factor out the 2: \(y = \cos(2(x - \pi/2))\), so the phase shift is \(\pi/2\) to the right.
  • Negative Radius in Polar Coordinates: \((-r, \theta)\) is plotted by moving in the opposite direction: \((-r, \theta) = (r, \theta + \pi)\).
  • Inverse Trig Ranges: \(\cos^{-1}(-1/2) = 2\pi/3\), NOT \(-2\pi/3\) or \(4\pi/3\), because the range of arccos is strictly \([0, \pi]\).

A tidal depth fluctuates sinusoidally with a high tide of 14 meters at 2:00 AM and a low tide of 6 meters at 8:00 AM. Write a cosine model \(h(t) = A\cos(B(t-c)) + d\) for water depth \(t\) hours after midnight.

Midline: \(d = \frac{14 + 6}{2} = 10\text{ meters}\).

Amplitude: \(A = \frac{14 - 6}{2} = 4\text{ meters}\).

Period: High to low tide takes 6 hours, so a full cycle is \(2 \times 6 = 12\text{ hours}\). Thus \(B = \frac{2\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}\).

Phase shift: High tide occurs at \(t = 2\), so \(c = 2\). Model: \[ h(t) = 4\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t - 2)\right) + 10. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

A sinusoidal function has a maximum at \((3, 18)\) and an adjacent minimum at \((9, 6)\). What are its amplitude, period, midline equation, and cosine formula \(y = A\cos(B(x-h))+k\)?

solution.en:
Amplitude: \[ A = \frac{18 - 6}{2} = \mathbf{6}. \]

Midline: \[ k = \frac{18 + 6}{2} = 12 \implies \mathbf{y = 12}. \]

Period: Half period is \(9 - 3 = 6\), so period \(T = 12\). Angular frequency: \[ B = \frac{2\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}. \]

Phase shift: Maximum is at \(x = 3\), so \(h = 3\). Equation: \[ \mathbf{y = 6\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(x - 3)\right) + 12}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Polar Coordinates, Polar Functions & Trigonometric Equations

body.en: Analyze curves defined in polar coordinates \(r = f(\theta)\), convert between polar and Cartesian forms, and solve quadratic-type trigonometric equations.

Coordinates \((r, \theta)\) represent distance \(r\) along a ray at angle \(\theta\) from the polar axis:

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad r^2 = x^2 + y^2, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}. \]

Rose curves: \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) or \(r = a\sin(n\theta)\) produces \(n\) petals if \(n\) is odd, and \(2n\) petals if \(n\) is even.

body.en:
Convert the polar equation \(r = 6\cos\theta\) to rectangular coordinates and identify the curve.

Multiply both sides by \(r\): \[ r^2 = 6r\cos\theta. \]

Substitute \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\) and \(r\cos\theta = x\): \[ x^2 + y^2 = 6x \implies x^2 - 6x + y^2 = 0. \]

Complete the square on \(x\): \[ (x - 3)^2 + y^2 = 9. \] This is a circle centered at \((3, 0)\) with radius 3.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Find all solutions to the trigonometric equation \(2\sin^2\theta - \sin\theta - 1 = 0\) on the interval \([0, 2\pi)\).

solution.en:
Factor as a quadratic in \(\sin\theta\): \[ (2\sin\theta + 1)(\sin\theta - 1) = 0. \]

Case 1: \(\sin\theta = 1 \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Case 2: \(2\sin\theta + 1 = 0 \implies \sin\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). In \([0, 2\pi)\), sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\): \[ \theta = \pi + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{7\pi}{6}, \quad \theta = 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{11\pi}{6}. \]

Solution set: \(\left\{ \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6} \right\}\).
